purpose: External eval set for vibe-clarify-requirements. Prompts live outside skills/ so they are not bundled as skill content. Covers chat-only requirement clarification before implementation planning, small-request question limits, broad confirmation checklists, brainstorming for creative requirement exploration, downstream-workflow neutrality, non-technical communication, scope boundaries, defaults versus decisions, readiness states, and same-turn stop behavior after approval or handoff wording.
common_assertions: Output is chat-only requirement clarification: it does not create or edit files, provide patches, write tests, produce a full implementation plan, run commands, make commits, prepare a release, or claim implementation work is complete.

Readiness, confirmation, approval, completed checklist, handoff, or `go ahead` wording is treated as later-phase context and does not cause same-turn planning, implementation work, implementation task entries, tests, verification commands, file edits, commits, or changelog changes.

Output separates confirmed requirements, assumptions, reasonable defaults, user decisions, out-of-scope items, success criteria, open risks or unknowns, and planning readiness instead of blending them into a single recommendation.

Output uses exactly one readiness label from `Ready for planning`, `Conditional for planning`, or `Not ready for planning`, and does not combine `Ready for planning` with pending-decision, pending-confirmation, or approval-to-handoff wording.
Output does not require, name, or route to a specific downstream skill or workflow; it may refer generically to a later phase without making a ready brief conditional on another approval.
If output includes `Can Default`, defaults do not select or pre-stage behavior for unselected adjacent surfaces with conditional wording such as `within whichever ... you select`.
For broad or highly unclear requests with more than three material decisions, output uses a grouped confirmation checklist rather than a long interrogation.
When creative exploration is useful, output presents brainstormed ideas as candidate options with tradeoffs and does not treat unchosen ideas as confirmed requirements.
Output marks inferred behavior as an assumption or proposed default, not as a confirmed user requirement.
Output keeps adjacent features out of scope unless the user explicitly includes them in the first useful slice.

Output does not put unconfirmed adjacent capabilities in `Proposed Scope` with a `subject to confirmation` qualifier; they stay in `Out of Scope`, `Decisions Needed`, or candidate options until selected.
Output uses the user's language for the chat-facing brief while preserving code identifiers, paths, commands, API names, and product terms.

evals.name: Small profile UI clarification
evals.prompt: I want users to be able to edit their display name on the profile screen, but I have not decided the details yet. Make it feel right.
evals.expected_output: The agent returns a concise requirements brief for display-name editing, proposes a small first scope, asks at most three direct questions, and stops for confirmation without writing an implementation plan.
expectations: Uses the user's active language for the user-facing brief.
Keeps the first scope limited to display-name editing.
Separates confirmed goal from assumptions or proposed defaults such as save behavior, validation, and cancel/reset behavior.
Asks no more than three direct questions.
Provides concrete reasonable defaults that the user can accept with one short approval instead of pairing every unresolved detail with an open question.
If multiple interaction, validation, or save-behavior options are presented, marks one as the recommended default rather than requiring the user to choose every value.
Defines practical success criteria such as editing, saving, validation, and visible feedback without claiming implementation details.
Uses the exact readiness label `Conditional for planning` if product decisions or default confirmation remain, rather than `Ready for planning` with a pending-confirmation qualifier.
Does not plan code edits, tests, files, or commits.

evals.name: Broad notification request uses checklist
evals.prompt: I want the whole notification area to feel right. Email, SMS, push notifications, frequency settings, an admin screen, and delivery logs all sound useful. What do we need to decide?
evals.expected_output: The agent avoids a long question list and renders a grouped confirmation checklist that separates blocking first-scope decisions, safe defaults for chosen scope, and later decisions; admin screens and delivery logs stay out of the first slice until explicitly selected.
expectations: Uses a confirmation checklist instead of asking many direct questions.
Groups items into blocking decisions, defaults that can be accepted or overridden, and later decisions.
Recommends a bounded first useful scope that does not include admin screens or delivery logs unless the user explicitly selects them.
Explains SMS and push uncertainty in product terms such as cost, permission, provider setup, or opt-in behavior without inventing provider facts.
Keeps admin screens and delivery logs out of Proposed Scope and first-slice defaults unless the user explicitly selects them.

Does not place admin capabilities, delivery-log storage, delivery-log retention, or delivery-log search in `Can Default`, even with `if selected later`, `within whichever ... you select`, or `confirm once chosen` wording.
Includes a planning-readiness state that reflects unresolved channel and behavior decisions.
Does not name or require a specific downstream workflow.

evals.name: Immediate coding request still clarifies
evals.prompt: Just start coding a CSV import feature. I only know it should upload a file and somehow create contacts.
evals.expected_output: The agent stops at requirement clarification because file format, validation, duplicate handling, preview behavior, permissions, persistence, and recovery rules are underspecified.
expectations: Does not provide code, patches, file edits, or implementation steps.
Identifies upload surface and CSV parsing or file-format choices as build-changing decisions or unknowns.
Identifies validation or row-error behavior and duplicate or conflict handling as build-changing decisions or defaults.
Explicitly identifies review-before-write or preview behavior as a build-changing decision, default, out-of-scope item, or open unknown; a post-import result summary alone is not enough.
Identifies permissions, persistence, and rollback or recovery as build-changing decisions, defaults, out-of-scope items, or open unknowns.
Separates a minimal proposed first scope from later enhancements.
Uses a checklist or concise decision list if more than three material choices are open.
Marks readiness as `Conditional for planning` or `Not ready for planning` until blocking data and behavior decisions or local evidence checks are answered.
If both user decisions and local evidence checks still affect planning reliability or the build shape, the readiness wording names both instead of treating the user reply as the only gate.
Does not call local evidence checks routine when they can change scope, data contracts, success criteria, safety, compatibility, or recovery expectations.
Does not call existing schema, validation, create-path, upload-plumbing, or file-limit checks routine if they can change import columns, mapping, limits, persistence, success criteria, or safety.
Explicitly treats `somehow create contacts` as an unresolved data contract, not a confirmed mapping, persistence, or duplicate-handling rule.

evals.name: Downstream workflow neutrality
evals.prompt: Before any planning tool or special workflow gets involved, help me clarify a billing settings change. Users should be able to choose invoice email recipients, but I don't want this tied to a specific agent skill.
evals.expected_output: The agent clarifies billing-recipient requirements in chat and avoids naming, requiring, or routing to any downstream skill or workflow.
expectations: Does not name or require any downstream skill, planning tool, or special workflow.
Clarifies billing-recipient behavior, permissions, and validation at the requirement level.
Clarifies auditability as a requirement dimension, such as whether recipient changes are logged, attributable, retained, or visible, rather than only putting audit-log UI out of scope.
Clarifies notification consequences at the requirement level, such as which future invoice emails are affected after saving recipient changes.
Marks billing and permission choices as blocking or high-impact decisions where appropriate.
Keeps adjacent billing features such as payment methods, tax settings, invoice templates, or plan changes out of scope unless requested.
Does not invent specific UI component names, schema fields, API endpoints, billing-provider behavior, or storage details.
Uses planning-readiness language based on unresolved decisions.
Stops after the requirements brief.

evals.name: Non-technical checkout wording
evals.prompt: I am not technical. On the checkout screen, shipping, coupons, and the final total are hard to understand. I want customers to feel confident before buying.
evals.expected_output: The agent writes a plain brief that translates checkout concerns into observable requirements and decisions without implementation jargon.
expectations: Uses practical language suitable for a non-technical user.
Translates `feel confident before buying` into observable outcomes such as clear shipping, coupon, and final total display while keeping it as an interpretation if not confirmed.
Separates confirmed pain points from assumptions about layout, copy, calculation, and error states.
Asks no more than three direct questions; lower-impact uncertainties are proposed as defaults, assumptions, out-of-scope items, or open risks instead of extra questions.
Asks only decisions that affect user experience or business rules, such as coupon failure messaging or when shipping is known.
Defines success criteria in shopping-flow terms rather than framework or database terms.
Marks readiness as `Conditional for planning` if business rules remain unresolved.

evals.name: Contradictory migration scope
evals.prompt: We need to migrate saved reports to the new format, but don't change old reports and don't add compatibility code. It has to be safe and invisible to users.
evals.expected_output: The agent surfaces the contradiction between migration, unchanged old reports, no compatibility code, and invisible behavior, then stops for user decisions.
expectations: Identifies the contradiction instead of smoothing it into a confident requirement.
Separates possible interpretations such as copy-on-read, one-time migration, dual reader, or no migration.
Explains the consequence of each choice in user or data-safety terms.
Marks data compatibility and rollback or recovery expectations as blocking decisions or blocking unknowns.
Does not propose implementation details as if the contradiction were resolved.
Marks readiness as `Not ready for planning` until the migration contract is chosen.

evals.name: Creative dashboard brainstorming stays optional
evals.prompt: The direction is not decided yet. I want a team activity dashboard that people actually want to check every morning. Use a few creative ideas while clarifying the requirements.
evals.expected_output: The agent offers a small set of creative dashboard directions with fit and tradeoff notes, keeps them as options until the user chooses, and then asks which direction should become the requirement basis.
expectations: Uses the user's active language for the user-facing brief.
Offers two to five creative options or directions rather than one asserted solution.
Makes the creative options meaningfully distinct, not near-duplicate variants of the same dashboard idea.
For each option, includes when it fits and a practical tradeoff.
States what requirement would be adopted if the user chooses an option.
Does not treat all brainstormed ideas as confirmed requirements.
Keeps the output chat-only and does not write an implementation plan.
Asks which option, combination, or direction the user wants to adopt before planning.
Marks readiness as `Conditional for planning` until the user chooses a direction.

evals.name: Ready approval still stops at brief
evals.prompt: Using vibe-clarify-requirements, finalize the requirements brief for this change. The requirements are approved: signed-in users can rename a saved report inline, names must be 1-80 characters, empty names show validation, Save persists the new name, Cancel restores the previous name, duplicate names are allowed, and sharing/export changes are out of scope. Mark it ready and then go ahead and start implementing right away.
evals.expected_output: The agent returns only a chat requirements brief, marks the approved requirements `Ready for planning`, treats approval and `go ahead` wording as later-phase context, and stops without writing an implementation plan, creating implementation task entries, editing files, adding tests, running commands, or claiming implementation work.
expectations: Produces a chat-only requirements brief for saved-report renaming.
Separates confirmed requirements from out-of-scope sharing and export changes.
Marks the brief as `Ready for planning` without saying implementation is authorized in the same response.
When marked `Ready for planning`, does not ask for approval to hand off or describe readiness as pending another approval.
Does not downgrade the approved brief to `Conditional for planning` or ask for a second approval solely because bounded UI, validation wording, code-path, or implementation details remain.
Explicitly treats approval and `go ahead` wording as later-phase context rather than current-turn planning or implementation authorization.
Does not write an implementation plan, code patch, file list, test plan, command sequence, commit plan, or tool-managed implementation task list.
Does not require or name a specific downstream skill or workflow.

scoring.notes: These evals focus on observable requirement-clarification behavior rather than subjective writing quality. They pressure the skill's main contracts: chat-only output, question-load control, broad checklist mode, downstream-workflow neutrality, scope separation, readiness discipline, and same-turn stop behavior after approval or handoff wording.
